10	### Terminal *content* accessibility (macapp) — CMT-3 — SHIPPED (2026-08-10)
11	
12	**Shipped:** `isAccessibilityElement()`/`accessibilityValue()` are real now (no longer gated behind
13	the UI-test fixture), a new `accessibilitySelectedText()` reads the existing `readSelectionText()`,
14	and a 400ms `Timer` poll posts coalesced `.valueChanged`/`.selectedTextChanged` only when the read
15	content actually changed. There is no render/damage callback on the libghostty side to hook instead
16	(checked `GhosttyRuntimeAdapter`'s full `GHOSTTY_ACTION_*` switch first) — the poll checks
17	`NSWorkspace.shared.isVoiceOverEnabled` FIRST on every tick, so the real cost (materializing the
18	viewport into a `String`) is paid only while VoiceOver is actually listening. The safety property
19	below (a password prompt must never leak through this) was verified empirically, not by reasoning
20	about terminal semantics: `TerminalAccessibilityUITests.testPasswordPromptWithEchoDisabledRendersNoTypedCharacters`
21	drives a real `stty -echo` + `read` prompt in a real pane and asserts the typed secret never appears
22	in the read viewport. Everything below this line is the pre-fix scoping and stays as the historical
23	record of what was decided and why.
24	
25	**What:** VoiceOver support for the terminal's *rendered text* on `GhosttySurfaceView` — accessible
26	value (screen text), selected text, and change notifications — so the terminal content is navigable
27	with assistive tech.
28	
29	**Done so far:** the **UI-tree** a11y has landed (commit `f3859f9`) — `PaneTreeView` exposes each
30	leaf as `terminal.pane` with a label ("Terminal <title>, pane N of M"), a focused/selected trait, and
31	an adjustable split divider (`pane.grip`). That claim is unqualified: the one caveat raised against it
32	(the tab strips' glyph buttons reporting `isHittable == false`) was investigated and closed as an
33	XCUITest artefact — see **Recently done**. What's still missing is the *content* layer: the
34	libghostty surface is Metal-rendered, so its text is pixels — invisible to the accessibility system.
35	Today the surface view sets `role=.textArea` + a label only; it exposes **no value and no selection**,
36	so VoiceOver reads nothing inside the terminal. Accepted regression for the beta (CMT-3). This is also
37	the **enabler for content-level UI tests**: once terminal text is in the a11y tree, XCUITest can
38	assert on rendered output (backspace deleted, TUI drew, scrollback) on top of the now-landed fixture
39	seam — see `macapp/QA-libghostty.md` (Bucket 2).
40	
41	**When:** feasible on the currently pinned engine today (the read APIs exist), but ghostty upstream
42	has merged a11y plumbing worth riding — **ghostty #12902** ("core: send selection_changed
43	notification", merged 2026-06-04), which on macOS posts `.ghosttySelectionDidChange` → debounced →
44	`NSAccessibility.selectedTextChanged`. On the pinned engine we'd have to post that notification
45	ourselves from our own selection events; after the pin bump it comes from the engine as
46	`GHOSTTY_ACTION_SELECTION_CHANGED`.

49	xcframework — an earlier version of this entry sequenced it behind CMT-2, which was wrong. A
50	before-GA item either way; doing it before the bump costs one self-posted notification.
51	
52	**How to start (minimal-viable, keep light per D1 — crib Muxy's `accessibilitySelectedText()`):**
53	- `accessibilityValue()` → visible screen text via `ghostty_surface_read_text(surface, <viewport
54	  ghostty_selection_s>, …)` (reuse the `extractString(from:)` helper).
55	- `accessibilitySelectedText()` → `ghostty_surface_read_selection` (the same read that powers
56	  copy-on-select).
57	- Post `NSAccessibility.post(element:notification:)` `.selectedTextChanged` on selection change
58	  (we already detect mouseUp / copy-on-select) and a throttled `.valueChanged` on output so
59	  VoiceOver follows along; keep the role/label and report focus.
60	- Skip the full `NSAccessibility` text protocol (line/char-range/bounds geometry) — overkill for a
61	  terminal, and Muxy keeps it minimal too.

101	### `workroom-session` daemon: the findings the `/review` pass didn't fix (macapp) — persist-sessions follow-up
102	
103	**What:** The `workroom-session` daemon (persisted ordinary terminals across quit, `b28e9134`) went
104	through a two-round `/review` (checklist + specialist dispatch, then a full Claude+Codex adversarial
105	pass). The three highest-value findings from round two were fixed directly (fallback-socket path
106	colliding across Workroom/Dev/Nightly builds, an off-by-one in
107	`PersistentSessionControlClient`'s own `sockaddr_un` length check that was one byte stricter than
108	the daemon's/attach-client's, and a `closeTab`-initiated kill racing an immediate quit). What's left,
109	in descending order of how much it matters:
110	
111	1. **The daemon reports a session as successfully created before `execve` runs.** `forkpty` returns
112	   the child PID immediately in the parent; the daemon acknowledges the client's `create`/`attach`
113	   at that point rather than waiting for the child to actually reach its shell. A child that fails
114	   between `fork` and `execve` (e.g. the target `cwd` vanished, `posix_spawn`-style setup failure)
115	   reports success and then the PTY silently closes moments later, rather than the client getting a
116	   clean failure up front.
117	2. **No connection-limit or reply-queue bound — a same-UID DoS vector.** Any process running as this
118	   user can open unboundedly many connections to the socket, and the daemon's per-connection outbox
119	   isn't capped, so a misbehaving or malicious same-UID client can exhaust descriptors or memory in
120	   the single-threaded daemon that every project's persisted terminals depend on.
121	3. **PID reuse after `waitpid` reaps a session's child.** Between the child exiting and the daemon
122	   noticing (via `reapChildren`), the OS is free to recycle that PID for an unrelated process; a
123	   narrow window exists where a stale `SIGHUP`/signal path could target the wrong process if any code
124	   keyed off the raw PID past that point rather than the PTY master descriptor.
125	4. **`SessionDescriptor.decodeList`'s wire encoding has no cap relative to `SessionFrame`'s max frame
126	   size.** A host with enough concurrent persisted sessions (many projects, many tabs) could in
127	   principle encode a `list` reply that exceeds the protocol's own frame-size ceiling, which would
128	   fail in a way nothing currently tests for.
129	5. **`setsid()`-spawned children can fork their own descendants that escape the daemon's forced
130	   cleanup.** `killpg` on the session's process group covers ordinary shell children, but a
131	   deliberately double-forking/re-`setsid`'d grandchild (rare, but not impossible from inside a
132	   persisted shell) can survive a `killAll`/teardown.
133	6. **`TerminalSessions.assignedSessionID`'s `isQuickTerminal` parameter is dead.** No caller passes
134	   `true` for it any more (the quick-terminal exclusion is handled elsewhere in
135	   `TerminalPersistentSessionPolicy` now) — cosmetic, but confusing for the next reader trying to
136	   figure out which layer actually excludes quick terminals.
137	
138	**P0 architectural note, accepted as-is (not a bug for this PR):** the daemon's only authentication
139	is `LOCAL_PEERCRED`/`peerUserID == getuid()` — any process running as the same user can list/attach/
140	kill any of that user's persisted sessions across every open project. This is the same threat model
141	tmux and screen have always had (a same-user socket is inherently shared trust), not a regression
142	this feature introduces, and items 1-3 above assume that same boundary rather than trying to harden
143	past it.
144	
145	**Why:** Residue of a two-round review (checklist + specialist dispatch, then Claude+Codex
146	adversarial) on a brand-new always-on daemon that every persisted terminal now depends on. None of
147	these are exploitable beyond the accepted same-UID trust boundary, and none causes silent data loss
148	in the common path — they're edge cases (process launch races, resource exhaustion, PID reuse
149	windows, an encoding ceiling, escaping cleanup, dead code) that are real but lower-value than the
150	three fixed directly.
151	
152	**Priority:** P2. Worth a pass if any of these starts showing up in the wild (a "session shows created
153	but the tab never attaches" report would point at #1; a "Workroom got slow/unresponsive with many
154	terminals open" report would point at #2).

592	### VCS write actions — Phase 2 (macapp) — roadmap pointer
593	
594	**What:** The next VCS phase: turn the read-only foundation into a full in-app VCS UI. **Fetch, push
595	and pull-with-rebase have SHIPPED** (the VCS toolbar), and so have **commit + message-only amend/describe**
596	(the Changes inspector's commit dialog). What remains: selection-aware amend (needs a temp index),
597	bookmark (jj) / branch (git) management, and the deep jj ops (undo/op-log, split, absorb, evolog,
598	interdiff).
599	
600	**Where the write seam actually is — this changed.** The original plan put write methods on
601	`VCSProviding` with a `CLIVCSProvider` fallback. That is **not** what shipped, and new work should not
602	follow it. Writes live behind a **separate** `VCSWriting` protocol (`Core/VCSWriting.swift`) with its
603	own factory `VCS.writer(for:)`, conformed by `CLIVCSWriter`. Two reasons, both load-bearing:
604	
605	- `VCSProviding`'s doc calls it "the single seam the app **reads** VCS data through", and four
606	  resolvers construct providers freely and call them with no gate. A `fetch` on that protocol means
607	  nothing structurally stops a read path firing a network mutation — the opposite of what
608	  `JJSnapshotGate` exists to guarantee.
609	- A CLI-backed method needs an injected `StatusCommandRunning`, and `GitProvider`/`RustJJProvider` are
610	  stateless value types constructed at four call sites with nowhere to put one. A new conformer has
611	  somewhere.
612	
613	So: add commit/amend and the rest as `VCSWriting` members, and they inherit the gate, the network
614	environment hardening and the failure taxonomy for free.
615	
616	**Which backend each op uses — decided, don't re-litigate.** `VCSWriting` says *where* writes live,
617	not *how* they run. The split:
618	
619	| Ops | Backend | Why |
620	|---|---|---|
621	| commit/amend — **CLI, decided against this table's original answer** | **CLI** (`CLIVCSWriter.commit`, shipped) | This row used to say "native", and that was wrong on three counts it never weighed. **libgit2 runs no hooks** ([#964](https://github.com/libgit2/libgit2/issues/964)) — a `pre-commit`/`commit-msg` that the user's terminal honours would be silently skipped, which is worse than not offering commit at all. **libgit2 cannot sign**, so `commit.gpgsign = true` would produce unsigned commits. And native jj commit is blocked on `immutable_heads()` being a jj-*cli* revset alias that jj-lib cannot resolve — so it would happily rewrite commits the user's own `jj` refuses to touch. (The empty-committer and dropped-signature halves of that third blocker are now fixed by `jj_config.rs`; the revset one is not.) |
622	| branch + bookmark management, jj undo/op-log/split/absorb/evolog | **native** (libgit2/SwiftGitX, jj-lib) — provisional | Local, typed APIs, no output to parse, no tool-version floor, no locale exposure. Still the default answer, but **not "don't re-litigate"**: commit was re-litigated on measurement and moved. Check each op for hooks, signing, and revset aliases before assuming native. |
623	| fetch, push, pull | **CLI** — permanently, not a stopgap | Three independent blockers, all verified from checked-out sources: SwiftGitX passes NULL options (`git_remote_fetch(remotePointer, nil, nil, nil)`, and `pull` is a `// TODO`), so it has no credential callback at all; **libgit2 implements no `credential.helper` protocol** — nothing in its `src` reads that config key, so native auth means reimplementing helper invocation ourselves; and jj-lib shells to `git` for remote ops anyway (that's where its `MINIMUM_GIT_VERSION` comes from), so a "native jj push" is a git subprocess wearing a Rust coat. |
624	
625	**Non-goal: Workroom does not store credentials.** No OAuth client, no keychain writes, no auth
626	prompt, no account concept. The user's own helpers (`osxkeychain`, GCM, `!gh auth git-credential`,
627	anything corporate) are the correct answer, and shelling out gets every host — including ones we've
628	never heard of — for free, with the same credentials their terminal uses. GitHub Desktop is the
629	instructive counterexample: it also shells out (via `dugite`, which bundles its own git), but blanks
630	your helpers and registers itself as `credential.helper=desktop` because being *the GitHub client* is
631	its product. The cost of that choice is `app/src/lib/generic-git-auth.ts` — a second credential store,
632	with its own prompt UI, keychain keys and invalidation, for every non-GitHub host. We are not that
633	product, and the app's one GitHub dependency (PR status) already rides `gh`'s own token.
634	
635	**When you do shell out, never parse prose.** `--porcelain`, `-z`, `%(…)`, `-T`, exit codes. Measured:
636	`Updates were rejected` becomes `Les mises à jour ont été rejetées` under `fr_FR.UTF-8`, so a prose
637	match loses the whole failure taxonomy for a non-English user. `StatusCommandRunner` pins `LC_ALL=C`
638	as a backstop; it is not the plan.
639	
640	*Filed, not planned:* bundling our own `git` the way `dugite` does would delete all of
641	`Core/VCSToolVersions.swift` — floor, probe, notification, per-VCS scoping. Real cost (universal
642	binary, notarization, ~40MB, and the Go CLI would want the same binary), so revisit only if the
643	version floor actually bites a user.
644	
645	**Why:** This is a roadmap phase, not a tactical follow-up. The authoritative scope + sequencing live
646	in the issue #59 plan; this entry is the pointer that makes it discoverable.
647	
648	**How to start:** Read `Core/VCSWriting.swift` — its doc comment carries the routing diagram, the
649	per-backend command table and the placement rules (fetch always runs at the project root, for both
650	backends; jj push too, because bookmarks are repo-global). The read layer blocks nothing. What's left
651	of the error taxonomy is one-sided (git still flattens to `.io`), and the stale-working-copy **repair**
652	is itself a write, so it belongs to this phase.
653	
654	**Depends on:** the VCS read foundation (shipped, Phase 1) and the write seam (shipped with the
655	toolbar). Spans `Core/VCSWriting.swift`, possibly `vcs/` (Rust) + `WrVcs` UniFFI for native jj ops, and
656	new write-flow UI.
657	
658	**Priority:** P2 (the product direction; large — see the plan for the real breakdown).

660	### `.task(id:)` cancellation is not reliably delivered on an in-place value swap (macapp) — measured 2026-08-13
661	
662	**What:** while fixing an `AvatarView` staleness bug (a stale in-flight fetch for author A landing
663	in `result` after the same slot switched to author B), the fix's first draft guarded on
664	`Task.isCancelled` — SwiftUI's documented behavior for `.task(id:)` is "if the id value changes,
665	SwiftUI cancels the previous task." Instrumented and measured directly (`Avatar.swift`, temporary
666	`lastCancelObserved` seam, since removed): for an in-place `subject` swap at a stable view-identity
667	slot (no `ForEach` re-keying, just a `@Published`/`@ObservedObject` value change), `Task.isCancelled`
668	read **`false`** throughout the outgoing task's remaining lifetime, even though a brand-new `.task`
669	invocation for the new value had already started and completed. The guard was dead code.
670	
671	**Fix applied there:** replaced it with a generation token — `@State private var activeTaskKey`,
672	written at the START of every `.task` invocation (before its `await`) and compared against the
673	invocation's own captured key before committing. `@State` survives the slot being reused (same
674	mechanism `result` itself already relies on), so whichever invocation started LAST always wins the
675	comparison, independent of whether SwiftUI ever delivers real cancellation. Red/green-verified:
676	reverting the token guard reproduces the exact original failure.
677	
678	**Why this is worth a standalone entry:** any OTHER `.task(id:)` in this codebase that guards a
679	stale-write race on `Task.isCancelled` alone is potentially relying on the same dead code. Grep for
680	`Task.isCancelled` near a `.task(id:` call before trusting one; the working pattern is the
681	generation-token comparison above, not the cancellation flag.
682	
683	**Priority:** informational — no other call site audited yet. Worth a pass if another stale-write bug
684	surfaces in a `.task(id:)`-driven view.
685	
686	### `withTimeout` doesn't observe the CALLER's own cancellation (macapp) — FIXED
687	
688	**Status:** the original version of this entry (a `withThrowingTaskGroup` awaiting a detached
689	operation child past its own deadline) is **fixed** — `Core/Timeout.swift` now races via a single
690	`withCheckedThrowingContinuation` + a `TimeoutGate`, exactly the fix this entry used to recommend.
691	Re-audited during the jj-snapshot-serialization `/review` (2026-07-24, cross-model: Codex found it)
692	and found a **different, still-live** gap in that same seam — **now also fixed.**
693	
694	**Fixed:** `withTimeout` wraps its continuation in `withTaskCancellationHandler` (a `TimeoutCancelBox`
695	bridges `onCancel`, which Swift can invoke before/during/after the continuation attaches, to settling
696	the SAME `TimeoutGate` early with a new `VCSCancellationError`) — same shape `JJSnapshotGate.run`
697	already used. `WorkroomStatusResolver`'s two catch sites treat `VCSCancellationError` the same as
698	`VCSTimeoutError`; `BranchResolver`'s blanket `catch` and `JJSnapshotGate`'s own `try?` call were
699	already safe either way. `TimeoutTests.swift` (previously zero coverage on this seam) covers the
700	success/deadline baselines plus both cancellation orderings (mid-race and already-cancelled-at-call)
701	and a 200-iteration stress test for the exactly-once settle guarantee; the cancellation test itself
702	proves the fix by needing well under 1s against a 5s deadline/operation, not the full wait. Full
703	`WorkroomStatusResolverTests`/`WorkroomStatusConcurrencyTests`/`BranchResolverTests`/
704	`VCSProviderConformanceTests` sweep green, no regressions.
705	
706	**What:** `withTimeout`'s `withCheckedThrowingContinuation` only resolves on ITS OWN internal race
707	(the operation finishing vs. its own `seconds` deadline firing) — it never wires up
708	`withTaskCancellationHandler`, so it does not observe the CALLING task being cancelled from outside.
709	Concretely: `AppStore+WorkroomStatus.swift`'s `statusSweepTask?.cancel()` (a new sweep replacing an
710	old one) propagates into `runLocalSweep`'s `withTaskGroup` children structurally, but a cancelled
711	child's in-flight `withTimeout(seconds:) { … }` call (inside `resolveJJ`/`resolveGit`) keeps running
712	to completion (or its own `seconds` timeout) regardless — it doesn't stop early just because the
713	enclosing task gave up.
714	
715	**Why:** Wastes CPU/time re-running a probe nobody wants anymore, and — post the jj-snapshot-gate
716	fix — adds unnecessary extra contention pressure on `JJSnapshotGate` (an unwanted, already-abandoned
717	caller still occupies a project's queue slot for up to its full timeout). This is a
718	responsiveness/efficiency gap, not a data-integrity one, because the call sites in this seam do
719	check `Task.isCancelled` before merging a stale result (`runLocalSweep`'s
720	`if Task.isCancelled { break }`, etc.).
721	
722	**Corrected 2026-08-05 — do NOT re-read this entry as "the convention protects us".** This used to
723	say *every* call site already checks, so state stays correct. That was false, and the counterexample
724	shipped: `refreshGitHubCLI` mutated `githubCLIStatus` **inside** an awaited function, where the
725	callers' own guards (`AppStore+WorkroomStatus.swift:86`/`:144`) run too late to help. A cancelled
726	probe's SIGKILLed `gh` still returned through `StatusCommandRunner`'s non-throwing continuation with
727	the signal number as its exit code, the classifier read that as "not signed in", and publishing it
728	*stamped the TTL* — so the wrong value suppressed its own repair for a full minute. The cost of a
729	missed guard is therefore a **wrong published value**, not merely a wasted probe. Two defences
730	landed with that fix and are what keeps the residual risk low: `CommandResult.signaled` (a killed
731	child is never mistaken for a CLI that ran and failed) and `GHAuthProbe.keepPrior` (a non-answer
732	neither writes nor stamps). The `withTimeout` gap below is a genuinely different mechanism and stays
733	deferred on its own merits.
734	
735	**Priority:** done.
736	
737	### VCS toolbar: the findings the `/review` pass didn't fix (macapp)
738	
739	**What:** Everything the toolbar review verified but left standing. Each was reproduced or read off the
740	code; none is speculative. Ordered by what a user hits first.
741	
742	**Nine have since SHIPPED and are struck below**, so the list is what remains:
743	
744	- **the empty-remote case** (was (1)): `CLIVCSWriter.mergeRemotes` now unions the configured remote list
745	  (`git remote`, `jj git remote list`) with the ref-derived names for both backends, so publishing to a
746	  brand-new empty remote works and the counts stay ref-derived.
747	- **(5), (6) and (7)** — the three a user noticed — see each entry.
748	
749	2. **jj Pull guesses `trunk()` as the base for an unbookmarked `@`.** Right for a workroom off trunk,
750	   wrong for one off a feature branch: it reports "N behind" counting trunk's commits and the rebase
751	   then refuses (`immutableHistory`, now typed and retry-free, so it fails honestly rather than looping).
752	   **Correction (2026-08-10): the "wrong for a feature branch" claim above does not reproduce.**
753	   Three ancestor-based revsets were tried against real jj repos while attempting a fix — `trunk() &
754	   ::@`, either-direction ancestry, and `(trunk()..@) & ::(immutable_heads())` — and all were falsified

101	### `workroom-session` daemon: the findings the `/review` pass didn't fix (macapp) — persist-sessions follow-up
102	
103	**What:** The `workroom-session` daemon (persisted ordinary terminals across quit, `b28e9134`) went
104	through a two-round `/review` (checklist + specialist dispatch, then a full Claude+Codex adversarial
105	pass). The three highest-value findings from round two were fixed directly (fallback-socket path
106	colliding across Workroom/Dev/Nightly builds, an off-by-one in
107	`PersistentSessionControlClient`'s own `sockaddr_un` length check that was one byte stricter than
108	the daemon's/attach-client's, and a `closeTab`-initiated kill racing an immediate quit). What's left,
109	in descending order of how much it matters:
110	
111	1. **The daemon reports a session as successfully created before `execve` runs.** `forkpty` returns
112	   the child PID immediately in the parent; the daemon acknowledges the client's `create`/`attach`
113	   at that point rather than waiting for the child to actually reach its shell. A child that fails
114	   between `fork` and `execve` (e.g. the target `cwd` vanished, `posix_spawn`-style setup failure)
115	   reports success and then the PTY silently closes moments later, rather than the client getting a
116	   clean failure up front.
117	2. **No connection-limit or reply-queue bound — a same-UID DoS vector.** Any process running as this
118	   user can open unboundedly many connections to the socket, and the daemon's per-connection outbox
119	   isn't capped, so a misbehaving or malicious same-UID client can exhaust descriptors or memory in
120	   the single-threaded daemon that every project's persisted terminals depend on.
121	3. **PID reuse after `waitpid` reaps a session's child.** Between the child exiting and the daemon
122	   noticing (via `reapChildren`), the OS is free to recycle that PID for an unrelated process; a
123	   narrow window exists where a stale `SIGHUP`/signal path could target the wrong process if any code
124	   keyed off the raw PID past that point rather than the PTY master descriptor.
125	4. **`SessionDescriptor.decodeList`'s wire encoding has no cap relative to `SessionFrame`'s max frame
126	   size.** A host with enough concurrent persisted sessions (many projects, many tabs) could in
127	   principle encode a `list` reply that exceeds the protocol's own frame-size ceiling, which would
128	   fail in a way nothing currently tests for.
129	5. **`setsid()`-spawned children can fork their own descendants that escape the daemon's forced
130	   cleanup.** `killpg` on the session's process group covers ordinary shell children, but a
131	   deliberately double-forking/re-`setsid`'d grandchild (rare, but not impossible from inside a
132	   persisted shell) can survive a `killAll`/teardown.
133	6. **`TerminalSessions.assignedSessionID`'s `isQuickTerminal` parameter is dead.** No caller passes
134	   `true` for it any more (the quick-terminal exclusion is handled elsewhere in
135	   `TerminalPersistentSessionPolicy` now) — cosmetic, but confusing for the next reader trying to
136	   figure out which layer actually excludes quick terminals.
137	
138	**P0 architectural note, accepted as-is (not a bug for this PR):** the daemon's only authentication
139	is `LOCAL_PEERCRED`/`peerUserID == getuid()` — any process running as the same user can list/attach/
140	kill any of that user's persisted sessions across every open project. This is the same threat model
141	tmux and screen have always had (a same-user socket is inherently shared trust), not a regression
142	this feature introduces, and items 1-3 above assume that same boundary rather than trying to harden
143	past it.
144	
145	**Why:** Residue of a two-round review (checklist + specialist dispatch, then Claude+Codex
146	adversarial) on a brand-new always-on daemon that every persisted terminal now depends on. None of
147	these are exploitable beyond the accepted same-UID trust boundary, and none causes silent data loss
148	in the common path — they're edge cases (process launch races, resource exhaustion, PID reuse
149	windows, an encoding ceiling, escaping cleanup, dead code) that are real but lower-value than the
150	three fixed directly.
151	
152	**Priority:** P2. Worth a pass if any of these starts showing up in the wild (a "session shows created
153	but the tab never attaches" report would point at #1; a "Workroom got slow/unresponsive with many
154	terminals open" report would point at #2).

input.new_string:
1. ~~**The daemon reports a session as successfully created before `execve` runs.**~~ **FIXED.**
   `SessionPTY.spawn` now uses the classic self-pipe trick: a `CLOEXEC` pipe created before
   `forkpty`, whose write end the child holds open only until `execve` either succeeds (the kernel
   closes it as part of the exec syscall) or fails (the child writes its `errno` and `_exit(127)`s).
   The parent's blocking read on the other end distinguishes the two synchronously — EOF means the
   child reached its shell, any bytes mean it didn't — so `spawn` now returns `nil` on a genuine
   exec failure and `create()`'s existing failure path (which already sent a clean `.failure` frame
   whenever `spawn` returned `nil`) fires instead of acking `.attached` and then closing moments
   later. Red/green-verified: `SessionDaemonEndToEndTests.testExecFailureReportsFailureNotSilentExit`
   (a nonexistent `shell` path forces a real `execve` failure) fails with the detection bypassed and
   passes with it restored, with no regression across the other 197 session/store tests.
2. ~~**No connection-limit or reply-queue bound — a same-UID DoS vector.**~~ **HALF-STALE, now
   FIXED.** The connection-count half was already capped (`maximumConnections = 64`, landed in an
   earlier round of this same review) — this entry hadn't been updated to reflect that. What was
   still genuinely open: protocol replies (`list`/`info`/`attach`/`kill`/`killAll`) are generated
   straight from client requests and aren't covered by the existing `clientOutputLimit` backpressure
   (which only gates output frames sourced from a session's pty), so a same-UID client that kept
   sending requests without ever reading its socket could grow a connection's outbox without bound.
   Fixed with a `connectionOutboxLimit` (8 MB, deliberately above `clientOutputLimit` so a client

input.new_string:
3. ~~**PID reuse after `waitpid` reaps a session's child.**~~ **FIXED, and the window was real, not
   theoretical.** `reapChildren`'s `waitpid` call REAPS the zombie — releasing its pid back to the
   OS's available pool — before it calls `endSession`, which used to call `closeMaster`, which
   unconditionally sent the session's process group a `SIGHUP`+`SIGCONT` via `SessionPTY.terminate`.
   Any `kill`/`killpg` issued after that reap targets whatever the OS may have already recycled that
   pid to, not the session's shell. The interleaving that triggers it is the ORDINARY case of a
   command that prints trailing output right before exiting: the pty keeps that output buffered
   until it's read, so the master fd doesn't report EOF (the OTHER path into `closeMaster`, which
   runs before `reapChildren` in the same event-loop turn and is therefore always safe — the pid is
   still an unreaped zombie at that point) until after `reapChildren`'s `waitpid` has already reaped
   it. Fixed by threading a `signalProcess` flag through `closeMaster`/`endSession`, defaulting to
   `true` everywhere except `reapChildren`'s call, which already knows — from the `waitpid` that just
   returned this exact pid — that there is nothing left to signal.
   `SessionDaemonEndToEndTests.testNaturalExitWithTrailingOutputReapsCleanly` exercises this precise
   interleaving (trailing output immediately before exit) end to end and pins the outcome: correct
   exit status delivered, session cleanly removed. It can't assert the skipped signal directly —
   nothing in the protocol surfaces that — so treat the code review (the vulnerable call site is
   simply gone from the reap path) as the other half of the verification, the same way other latent
   races in this file are closed by reasoning plus a behavioral pin rather than a flaky repro.

input.new_string:
5. ~~**`setsid()`-spawned children can fork their own descendants that escape the daemon's forced
   cleanup.**~~ **FIXED, and the first attempt exposed a second, sharper bug.** `killpg` (the soft
   `terminate()` used by `closeMaster`) and the old `getsid`-based matching (`forceTerminate`) both
   scope by session/group, so a deliberately double-forking/re-`setsid`'d grandchild — now the
   leader of a session nothing was tracking — escaped both. Fixed with a one-time, upfront
   parent-pid tree walk (`SessionPTY.descendantProcessIDs`, sharing a `snapshotProcesses()` scan
   with the existing `sessionProcessIDs`): every transitive descendant of the root pid is tracked
   as its own additional signal target, found by ancestry rather than by whatever
   session/group it has since made itself leader of.
   **What the first version of this fix missed, caught by the regression test itself:** `endSession`/
   `endSessions` call `closeMaster` (the soft `killpg`+`SIGHUP`) BEFORE `forceTerminate` — and SIGHUP's
   default disposition is terminate, so that soft signal was reliably killing the session's shell
   moments before `forceTerminate`'s own tree-walk snapshot ran, reparenting the detached grandchild to
   launchd and erasing the very parent-pid link the walk depends on. The real fix needed the snapshot to
   happen before ANY signal in the sequence, not just before the hard one — `closeMaster` now takes a
   `signalProcess` flag (added for the PID-reuse fix above) and both force-path callers suppress the
   soft signal, since `forceTerminate` immediately following is both more thorough and (with this fix)
   the thing that actually needs to see the tree intact.
   Red/green-verified with a REAL detached grandchild, not a simulation:
   `SessionDaemonEndToEndTests.testKillAllReachesASetsidGrandchild` spawns a shell that backgrounds a
   perl process calling `setsid()`, confirms it's alive from outside the daemon, sends `.killAll`, and
   asserts the grandchild's pid is actually gone. Fails (reproducing survival) with either half of the
   fix reverted on its own, passes with both restored.

**What:** File upstream: `plan-eng-review`, `plan-ceo-review` and `plan-design-review` never got the
codex timeout wrapper their own CHANGELOG claims is universal, and `--enable web_search_cached` is
deprecated in codex 0.146.0.

the command sandbox; a fixed invocation runs in 104s. `CHANGELOG.md` claims "every `codex exec` /

`_gstack_codex_timeout_wrapper` uses (`codex/SKILL.md` uses 330s, `autoplan/SKILL.md` 600s). Codex
0.146 also prints `deprecated: [features].web_search_cached … web search is enabled by default`, so the
flag silently bought live web search that a plan review never wanted, at 10 call sites.

**Second, larger finding:** `/codex` and `/autoplan` call `_gstack_codex_timeout_wrapper` from Bash
blocks that never `source` the probe. Bash functions do not survive across tool calls — the probe file
says so itself — so the wrapper is undefined there and the invocation dies with exit 127. This likely
explains the review-log entries recording `"source":"claude"` instead of `"source":"codex"`: the codex
call fails and the skill silently falls back to the Claude subagent.

**Pros:** fixes it for every gstack user; our local patch survives `gstack-upgrade` only if upstream
takes it.

**Cons:** upstream may have context we lack for why those three were left on a bare Bash timeout.

**Also worth reporting, but to Claude Code rather than gstack:** `sandbox.excludedCommands: ["codex"]`
in `~/.claude/settings.json` does not exempt codex from the *filesystem* sandbox — verified, a bare
`codex` command still had a `/tmp` write denied. The working fix was adding `~/.codex` to
`sandbox.filesystem.allowWrite` (codex fails with `failed to initialize in-process app-server client:
Operation not permitted` without it).

input.new_string:
5. ~~**`setsid()`-spawned children can fork their own descendants that escape the daemon's forced
   cleanup.**~~ **FIXED, and the first attempt exposed a second, sharper bug.** `killpg` (the soft
   `terminate()` used by `closeMaster`) and the old `getsid`-based matching (`forceTerminate`) both
   scope by session/group, so a deliberately double-forking/re-`setsid`'d grandchild — now the
   leader of a session nothing was tracking — escaped both. Fixed with a one-time, upfront
   parent-pid tree walk (`SessionPTY.descendantProcessIDs`, sharing a `snapshotProcesses()` scan
   with the existing `sessionProcessIDs`): every transitive descendant of the root pid is tracked
   as its own additional signal target, found by ancestry rather than by whatever
   session/group it has since made itself leader of.
   **What the first version of this fix missed, caught by the regression test itself:** `endSession`/
   `endSessions` call `closeMaster` (the soft `killpg`+`SIGHUP`) BEFORE `forceTerminate` — and SIGHUP's
   default disposition is terminate, so that soft signal was reliably killing the session's shell
   moments before `forceTerminate`'s own tree-walk snapshot ran, reparenting the detached grandchild to
   launchd and erasing the very parent-pid link the walk depends on. The real fix needed the snapshot to
   happen before ANY signal in the sequence, not just before the hard one — `closeMaster` now takes a
   `signalProcess` flag (added for the PID-reuse fix above) and both force-path callers suppress the
   soft signal, since `forceTerminate` immediately following is both more thorough and (with this fix)
   the thing that actually needs to see the tree intact.
   Red/green-verified with a REAL detached grandchild, not a simulation:
   `SessionDaemonEndToEndTests.testKillAllReachesASetsidGrandchild` spawns a shell that backgrounds a
   perl process calling `setsid()`, confirms it's alive from outside the daemon, sends `.killAll`, and
   asserts the grandchild's pid is actually gone. Fails (reproducing survival) with either half of the
   fix reverted on its own, passes with both restored.

Committed: `0ab1f3c4`.

Now, the first P3, in plain English:

**"Gate git VCS reads, not just writes"**

Each project's workrooms are separate git worktrees all sharing one underlying `.git` folder. Writing operations (commit, push, pull) already go through a traffic-light system (`JJSnapshotGate`) so two writes on the same project never collide — that part's solid.

The gap: reading status (the little indicators showing what's changed, ahead/behind counts, etc.) does NOT go through that same traffic light for git projects — only for jj ones. So if the app is quietly polling status across every open workroom for a project (which it does regularly in the background) at the exact moment a fetch/pull is writing to the shared git internals, they can collide. Git briefly locks an internal file (`packed-refs`) while updating it; if the status-read touches that file at the same instant, it fails with a lock error. Because there's no gate on reads, the app treats that as an unexpected error, not something it anticipated and could just quietly retry — which is why the UI shows a "try again" option in a case that should really just be invisible plumbing.

Not GA-blocking, no data loss, but the workaround (adding reads to the gate) risks slowing down the background status sweep, so nobody's implemented it yet without first confirming how often it actually bites.

Committed: `745082ff`.

Now the next one, **"jj sibling-workspace staleness after a rebase"**, in plain English:

A jj project can have multiple workrooms open on it at once — each is its own "workspace" pointing into the same underlying repo. When you rebase in ONE workroom, jj updates that workroom's own view of history, but doesn't automatically tell the OTHER open workrooms (siblings) that the ground shifted under them. Their cached view of the repo goes stale.

The nasty part: this doesn't show up as an obvious "hey, refresh me" message. Instead, the SIBLING workroom just starts throwing a confusing, unrelated-looking error the next time you do something in it — so if you rebase in workroom A, you might go to workroom B five minutes later, hit an error there, and have no idea it's actually because of what you did in A. It's a wrong-place error, not a wrong-time one — genuinely confusing to debug from the user's side, since the cause and the symptom are in two different windows.
So what’s the solution?

content.text:
The fix isn't invent-from-scratch — the pieces mostly already exist, they're just not connected for this case:

1. **Detecting it's cheap and already built.** The app already has a specific error type (`staleWorkingCopy`) and already recognizes it when jj reports a stale workspace. The detection logic exists — it just currently only fires when the USER happens to run a command in the stale workroom and hits the error live.

2. **The missing piece is proactive checking of workrooms nobody's looking at.** Right now nothing checks sibling workrooms in the background after a rebase — they only find out when the user stumbles into them and something breaks. The fix is to have the app notice staleness for a workroom that ISN'T currently focused, not just react when it blows up in your face.

3. **The repair is a single existing jj command** (`jj workspace update-stale`) — so once staleness is detected, the fix is just: surface it ("this workroom is out of date because of a rebase elsewhere") and offer a button that runs that one command.

The tradeoff holding it back: checking every sibling workroom after every pull would add real cost (reading N workspaces per pull instead of one), so it needs a cheap way to know something's stale without eagerly re-reading everything — that's the actual unsolved design question, not the detection or the repair.
If the workroom is not focused, why would we need to react to it? Just react to it. Only when we need to or when it's focused.

half may largely exist; the gap is noticing it for a workroom the user is NOT looking at, and offering
the repair. The repair is itself a write, so it belongs on `VCSWriting`.
